entry.title: How APK Sentinel keeps Android APK analysis client-side

link.title: How APK Sentinel keeps Android APK analysis client-side

entry.content:
APK Sentinel is a browser-based defensive cybersecurity tool for authorized Android APK static analysis. The project is designed around a simple boundary: inspect a sample without uploading, installing, or executing it.

What the tool examines

The current workflow extracts permissions, endpoints, and suspicious indicators from an APK and presents them alongside an explainable heuristic risk score. The result is a downloadable JSON report that keeps the inspected signals visible instead of presenting a score without context.

This makes APK Sentinel a practical JavaScript and Android-security project, not a claim of complete malware detection. Static indicators are useful for triage and learning; they should be combined with appropriate authorization, sandboxing, and deeper analysis before anyone makes a security decision.

Why the project matters

The project connects several areas I am actively exploring: client-side web development, Android security, static analysis, and secure software design. Its public project page and source repository provide the best way to inspect the current implementation and follow future changes.

Open APK Sentinel
View the source on GitHub

What I plan to document next

Future notes can cover the file parsing boundary, how indicators are presented to users, how false positives should be explained, and which improvements are appropriate for an educational browser tool. Each update will be tied to a visible implementation change or a clearly labeled experiment.
entry.summary: A project note on APK Sentinel's browser-based static analysis workflow, explainable heuristic scoring, and downloadable JSON reports.

entry.title: Bazaro: a React and Vite commerce application study

link.title: Bazaro: a React and Vite commerce application study

entry.content:
Bazaro is a React and Vite e-commerce web application built with Supabase and PostgreSQL. The project records practical work across product browsing, authentication, cart management, and order placement without presenting unverified production metrics or sales results.

The implementation focus

The frontend uses React and Vite for the application interface. Supabase and PostgreSQL provide the database-backed foundation for product data, authentication, cart state, and orders. The project also documents the relationship between a responsive interface and the data rules needed to keep an e-commerce workflow understandable and controlled.

What to inspect

When reviewing the source, look at how product data reaches the interface, how authentication participates in the shopping flow, and how cart and order actions are represented. The project is a verifiable implementation record; it is not a claim about a live commercial store, customer volume, revenue, or conversion performance.

Technology context

  • React and Vite frontend
  • Supabase authentication and database services
  • PostgreSQL-backed product and order data
  • Product browsing, cart management, and order placement
  • Responsive interface structure and security-aware data access patterns

View the project page
View the source on GitHub

Next documentation step

A future revision can add screenshots, route details, and deployment notes after those details are documented directly from the repository and any public demo is available.
entry.summary: A project case study on Bazaro, a React and Vite e-commerce application using Supabase, PostgreSQL, authentication, cart management, and order placement.

entry.title: RSL E-commerce Clothing: a typed Next.js storefront study

link.title: RSL E-commerce Clothing: a typed Next.js storefront study

entry.content:
RSL E-commerce Clothing is a responsive clothing e-commerce web application built with Next.js and TypeScript. The project focuses on the frontend problem behind a storefront: make product browsing feel clear on different screen sizes while keeping the codebase typed and maintainable.

The implementation focus

The project uses a Next.js application structure and TypeScript-based development. Its published scope includes product browsing, reusable interface components, responsive frontend design, and a modern shopping experience. These choices make the project a useful record of practical React, Next.js, TypeScript, and e-commerce interface work.

This is a frontend project description, not a claim about a live store, production sales, or conversion results. A public live demo is not currently listed; the source repository is the verifiable implementation record.

What to inspect

When reviewing the project, look for how the interface separates reusable UI from page-level composition, how product information is presented, and how the responsive layout adapts across viewport sizes.

View the project page
View the source on GitHub

Next documentation step

The next useful addition is a short architecture note with screenshots, route structure, and the exact component decisions used for the product browsing flow. That information will be added when the implementation details are documented from the repository itself.
entry.summary: A project case study on RSL E-commerce Clothing, a responsive Next.js and TypeScript storefront focused on product browsing and maintainable frontend structure.
